    Joint Application for Authorization under Section 203

        COMMENTS OF THE VIRGINIA OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL,
                     DIVISION OF CONSUMER COUNSEL



                                               INTRODUCTION

           Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or the “Commission”)

August 25, 2026 Notice of Extension of Time, 1 the Virginia Office of the Attorney General,

Division of Consumer Counsel (“Virginia Consumer Counsel”) respectfully files these comments

regarding the proposed merger of NextEra Energy, Inc. (“NextEra”) and Dominion Energy, Inc.

(“Dominion”) (collectively, “Applicants”). Virginia Consumer Counsel is charged under Va. Code

§ 2.2-517 with “represent[ing] the interests of the people [of Virginia] as consumers.”2 In carrying

out this charge, Virginia Consumer Counsel is authorized to “[a]ppear before governmental

 commissions, agencies, and departments . . . to represent and be heard on behalf of Virginia

           This proposed merger would form the largest electric utility and power company in the

country at a time when skyrocketing prices, rapid load growth, and new technologies are

necessitating fundamental changes to the regulatory structure governing such entities. The new

proposed entity would operate within the regional wholesale markets and transmission planning

area of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”). The Commission has already raised serious

concerns about the impacts of large loads in the PJM market, and there are multiple proceedings

underway to protect consumers in PJM territory in the context of this rapid growth and associated

demands on the grid.4 Until PJM and its stakeholders, and the Commission, complete these related

analyses, the potential risks and merits of the proposed merger cannot be reasonably evaluated.

           In this case, Applicants bear the burden of demonstrating that the proposed merger is in the

public interest. In order for the Applicants to be able to make that showing, the record in this case

must be further developed with additional analysis.5 The public interest also demands a rigorous

analysis of how near-term changing market conditions and regulatory frameworks may amplify or

distort the potential impacts of the proposed merger on ratepayers. Without performing a forward-

looking market screen, the scope of the proposed merger’s direct and indirect impacts remain

unclear. The commitments Applicants have proposed are necessary protections to insulate

ratepayers from transaction costs but may not be sufficient to adequately protect customers from

aspects of the proposed merger in light of changing market conditions and regulatory structures in

order to effectively evaluate potential impacts of the transaction and ensure ratepayers are

protected.

                                               COMMENTS

      I.    Procedural Background and Application Status
           On July 15, 2026, NextEra and Dominion submitted an Application pursuant to sections

203(a)(1) and 203(a)(2) of the Federal Power Act6 and Part 33 of the Commission’s regulations7

seeking Commission authorization for a merger transaction. 8 As the statutorily designated

advocate for Virginia consumers, Virginia Consumer Counsel intervened.9 In the Application, the

Applicants assert that the merger would have “no adverse effects” on rates or competition and

make commitments to protect ratepayers from bearing certain transaction-related costs. On July

15, 2026, the Applicants also filed a petition with the Virginia State Corporation Commission

(“SCC”) seeking approval of an acquisition of control under Case No. PUR-2026-00112 to

approve the acquisition by NextEra of Dominion utilities operating in Virginia, and they have

made various commitments in that proceeding as well.

Docket No. EC26-131 (July 15, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260715-5205 (“Application”).

for reliability, retail ratemaking, transmission planning, and wholesale market operations, Virginia

Consumer Counsel joined other consumer advocates and attorneys general in filing a motion for

an extension of time to submit comments on the Application. 10 On August 25, 2026, the

Commission provided a fifteen-day extension of time for comments, protests, and interventions,

setting the deadline as September 29, 2026.

           On September 23, 2026, the Commission’s Office of Energy Market Regulation issued a

deficiency letter to the Applicants, posing questions about the entities, destination markets, and

effects on rates. 11 The effect of this issuance on the comment deadline in this proceeding is

unclear.12 Although the Application has been deemed incomplete, Virginia Consumer Counsel

submits these comments now out of an abundance of caution to ensure that there is no ambiguity

regarding the Commission’s obligation to protect ratepayers through its evaluation of the

Application, when and if it is deemed complete. Virginia Consumer Counsel notes that the

September 23 Deficiency Letter asks for additional information and identifies data discrepancies

around aspects of the Application that are at the core of Virginia Consumer Counsel’s comments.

Accordingly, Virginia Consumer Counsel reserves the right to file comments as additional

     II.    Applicable Law
           FERC reviews utility mergers under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act using a single

overarching standard: whether the transaction is consistent with the public interest. 13 The

Commission performs this evaluation using four safeguards, laid out in FERC’s Merger Policy

Statement and subsequent regulatory and legislative updates. 14 First, FERC examines the

transaction’s effects on competition, including market concentration, vertical market power, and

the ability of the merged entity to raise prices or foreclose rivals. Second, FERC reviews the

transaction’s effects on rates, requiring Applicants to demonstrate no adverse wholesale rate

impacts or to provide protections such as the hold harmless commitments, which ensure that

Applicants will not pass any transaction-related costs on to ratepayers.15 Third, FERC assesses

effects on regulation, ensuring that the transaction does not impair federal or state oversight and

that corporate structures remain transparent. Finally, FERC requires a specific showing that the

transaction will not result in inappropriate cross-subsidization of non-utility affiliates under the




13
     16 U.S.C. § 824b(a)(4).
14

592, 61 Fed. Reg. 68,595 (Dec. 30, 1996), FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,044 (1996), reconsideration denied, Order No.
592-A, 62 Fed. Reg. 33,341 (June 19, 1997), 79 FERC ¶ 61,321 (1997) (“Merger Policy Statement”).
15
   See, e.g., Liberty Utilities Co., 181 FERC ¶ 61,212, P 46 (2022) (“We also note that Applicants’ commitment to
hold their customers harmless from costs related to the Proposed Transaction is not a substitute for identifying the
effects of the Proposed Transaction on rates and demonstrating that such effects are not adverse.”); El Paso Electric
Company, 170 FERC ¶ 61,280, PP 54-55 (2020) (“We interpret Applicants’ hold harmless commitment to apply to
all transaction-related costs, including costs related to consummating the Proposed Transaction, incurred prior to the

accordance with the Commission’s policy on hold harmless commitments.”).

 Energy Policy Act of 2005.16 Together, these components form the modern FERC public interest

test applied in every Section 203 merger proceeding.

           FERC’s evaluation is “focus[ed] on ratepayer protection.”17 As stated in the Merger Policy

Statement, “[t]he applicant bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that the customer will be

protected[,]” and the applicant bears the risk that benefits will not materialize—putting the risk

“where it belongs.”18 FERC is required to act on the application within 180 days of filing, either

by granting, denying, or issuing an order tolling the time to act on the application by up to an

additional 180 days if it “finds, based on good cause, that further consideration is required to

determine whether the proposed transaction meets the [statutory] standards.”19

 III.       Argument
            a. The risk of harm to consumers caused directly or indirectly by the proposed
               merger cannot be properly evaluated until PJM consumer protection reforms are
               in place.
           The proposed merger comes at a time when utilities and regional transmission

organizations (“RTOs”) around the country are grappling with the investments needed to meet

rapid growth of large load customers – investments that the proposed merger seeks to capture.20

PJM’s challenges, in particular, are emblematic of the regulatory challenges presented by this

growth as PJM, states, and stakeholders work to develop approaches to mitigate cost impacts and

                                                           6
 the risks of stranded costs for other customers. It is not possible to evaluate the potential impacts

of the proposed merger without greater clarity surrounding PJM’s changing regulatory framework.

In PJM territory, as the Commission recently explained, “the size and speed with which data

centers can be connected to the grid present unique challenges for demand forecasting and system

planning.”21 There are a number of proceedings underway aimed at ensuring affordable, reliable,

and secure energy as large loads seek to connect to the grid within PJM. While the outcomes of

these proceedings are expected to present a way forward for the region, the current timeline and

structure of the proposed merger exacerbate the potential risk of harm to customers.

           In December 2025, FERC found that PJM’s tariff was unjust and unreasonable with respect

to co-located load and generation, reflecting a growing concern that the existing tariff framework

was not designed for the scale and volatility of data center demand and may result in shifting costs

onto other transmission customers.22 FERC based this finding on the tariff’s failure to specify clear,

consistent rates, terms, and conditions for co-located load arrangements, leading to the potential

for undue discrimination or preferential treatment. In January 2026, PJM filed its compliance

package, proposing revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff to reduce costs and timelines

for co-located generation by clarifying: (a) how generators serving co-located load could use

provisional interconnection service to begin operations before all required network upgrades are

done; (b) how interconnection service below nameplate capacity could be granted to study the

service level requested rather than the generator’s maximum possible output; and (c) how surplus

interconnection service for a facility that does not operate continuously could be used to support




21
  Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large Loads, Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking,
Docket No. RM26-4-000 (discussing NERC report about demand growth).
22

 new facilities serving co-located load.23 These revisions could allow for faster interconnection and

avoiding new builds where possible. FERC accepted portions of that filing but directed PJM to

make additional compliance filings, making clear that the RTO’s work was not finished.

           FERC also issued a more recent show cause order identifying the need for large load-

related reforms beyond those paired with generation. In this June Show Cause Order, FERC

identified that PJM’s processes require protections for wholesale transmission customers from cost

shifting, and the Commission directed PJM and its transmission owners to reevaluate how their

tariffs handle rapid, concentrated demand growth.24 PJM sought more time to respond to the June

Show Cause Order, which FERC granted, so it is expected that PJM will file a comprehensive

package of reforms in November 2026. 25 As a result, PJM’s comprehensive framework for

allocating the costs and risks of large-load growth will not be filed until after the comment deadline

in this merger proceeding. This leaves the Commission to evaluate the proposed merger against a

regulatory backdrop that is necessarily in flux, yet crucial to understanding the impacts of the

merger.

           FERC’s efforts to protect consumers from unfair cost allocations driven by the investments

needed to serve new large loads become even more challenging because this proposed merger

involves one of the largest merchant developers in the country and one of the most load-dense

regulated utilities in PJM. While FERC has found that the existing tariff framework in PJM was

not designed for the scale and volatility of data center-driven demand, a stated purpose of the

        Prior to the Commission taking any action on this Application, the public interest requires

that the Commission, ratepayers, and other stakeholders have more visibility into proffered

solutions to the problems that FERC has identified in the PJM market. A thorough understanding

of PJM’s market conditions and treatment of large loads is required for adequately assessing public

interest in regards to this transaction, and such understanding will only be possible after there is

more clarity on how the Commission will approach PJM’s November 2026 filing.

         b. FERC should undertake a forward-looking evaluation of the market power
            concerns presented by the proposed merger.
        In order to address the serious market power concerns presented by the proposed merger,

the Commission should undertake a rigorous, forward-looking review of the market conditions

affected by the merger. The Commission should also direct the Applicants to prepare a market

power screen that includes all known, quantifiable future development within the relevant

geographic areas.

        Dominion and its subsidiaries own transmission lines and electric generation, serve load,

and participate in the PJM market as both sellers and buyers.28 NextEra participates in the PJM

competition in PJM, and that analysis should account for material affiliated generation that is

           The Commission’s public interest mandate hinges on a clear, transparent, and adversarial

evaluation of the competitive effects of a merger, and market power should be examined with

respect to both generation and transmission. The Delivered Price Test and associated market power

screens are not mere procedural formalities; they are the analytical backbone of FERC’s

competition review under Order No. 592.34 When Applicants submit market analyses, the public

interest requires that those screens be subject to full scrutiny, including verification of input

assumptions, geographic market definitions, transmission constraints, and load-flow modeling.

Without rigorous review, the Commission risks accepting screens that mask localized market

power, understate concentration, or rely on optimistic dispatch assumptions that do not reflect real

operating conditions. Market power screens should encompass both in service and anticipated

generation and transmission projects.

           NextEra’s development posture in PJM is central to this analysis. Although the merger

Application emphasizes that NextEra currently owns only a modest amount of operating

generation in PJM,35 this claim is selective and misleading. NextEra Energy Resources has long

maintained one of the largest forward development pipelines in the region, with extensive queue

positions, transmission-dependent project sites, and active participation in PJM’s evolving

interconnection and transmission planning processes. For example, NextEra’s South Mon project

in southwestern Pennsylvania, mentioned above, would add 4.3 GW of gas-fired generation, more

alone would reflect a transformation in the competitive landscape in ways that cannot be captured

by static screens.

        The load side of the equation is even more consequential. Dominion’s Northern Virginia

service territory is the epicenter of load growth and data center expansion in the United States.39

Virginia’s data center expansion has already been occurring at scale and spreading well beyond

the Northern Virginia corridor. As of July 2026, Dominion reported approximately 53.8 GW of

data center capacity in various stages of contracting, more than triple the 16.5 GW it reported in

July 2023.40 Treating this transaction as if it were merely a combination of existing assets would

In other words, the transaction is expressly designed to reshape future load and future supply

simultaneously. That is the textbook definition of a forward-looking competitive effect that must

be analyzed under FERC regulations.42

         Ignoring the dynamic nature of the variables in the market screen would mean ignoring the

exact conditions that FERC has identified as requiring heightened attention. The combination of

Dominion’s regulated load obligations and NextEra’s merchant development pipeline creates a

vertically integrated entity with the ability and incentive to coordinate future generation siting,

queue positioning, and transmission development in ways that affect market outcomes for captive

customers. Even if no affiliate sales occur, future NextEra projects can still set prices paid by

Dominion’s retail load given the scope of the assets involved. Future transmission constraints and

retirements in PJM could amplify that effect. These are not speculative concerns; they are the

foreseeable consequences of the merger’s stated purpose and thus must be appropriately

analyzed.43

            A forward-looking market analysis is therefore not an optional enhancement to the standard

Section 203 review, but rather it is the only method capable of capturing the competitive effects

of a transaction whose value lies almost entirely in the future. FERC’s own recent orders,44 PJM’s

documented load conditions, and NextEra’s development posture all represent reasons why the

merger must be evaluated based on the market that will exist after the pieces of the combined entity

begin building the projects and serving the load that motivated the transaction in the first place.

Because static market power screens cannot address these market power concerns, a

forward-looking competitive analysis would be the most appropriate way to evaluate the market-

related impacts of the proposed transaction.

           Equally important, affected parties must have a meaningful opportunity to comment on

those market-power screens and any proposed mitigation strategies before the Commission makes

a finding on the Application. FERC’s rules are designed to ensure that intervenors can test the

more realistic market definitions, or to demonstrate that mitigation measures are insufficient or

improperly tailored. Because market-power determinations directly affect wholesale customers,

state commissions, and regional market participants, the Commission does not have a sufficient

record at this time to proceed with analyzing the proposed merger. Until forward-looking market

screens are available to interested parties to review and comment upon, the Commission should

not finalize its competitive effect findings.

interest determination rests on a complete and reliable evidentiary record.

impact state regulation because it will cause no change to the regulatory authority of the [Virginia

SCC] and the [North Carolina Utilities Commission] over VEPCO, the [South Carolina Public

Service Commission] over DESC, or the Florida Public Service Commission . . . over FPL.”59 This

oversimplification ignores the regulatory burden that will increase from the expansive scope and

                                        CONCLUSION

       Virginia Consumer Counsel respectfully requests that the Commission: (a) not make a

determination on the Application until the Commission’s analysis can be informed by the

resolution of other proceedings related to large load issues in PJM; (b) base its determination in

this proceeding on a forward-looking market screen to capture an accurate scope of market power

held by the merged entity; (c) if it approves the Application, make binding and enforceable the

commitments made by the Applicants and consider additional conditions necessary to ensure that

the transaction is in the public interest; and (d) give full consideration to the proposed merger’s

potential impacts on state regulation by allowing the Virginia SCC merger proceeding to inform

the Commission’s evaluation.
